dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.5.pla: To produce one unit, England needs 100 hours for cloth and 120 for wine; Portugal needs 90 for cloth and 80 for wine [19].
Portugal is better at both, but its lead is much bigger for wine (80 versus 120) than for cloth (90 versus 100).
Portugal specializes in wine, England in cloth, and they trade.
With the same number of working hours, both countries end up with more wine and more cloth than if they produced everything themselves [19].
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.6.tit: The 19th century: English wheat and French candles
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.6.par: In the United Kingdom, the ==“Corn Laws”== tax imported wheat to protect big landowners. Bread is expensive, and urban workers suffer. After a long battle led by the Anti-Corn Law League and the famine in Ireland, Prime Minister Robert Peel repeals them in ==1846==. The United Kingdom becomes the champion of free trade.

In France, the economist ==Frédéric Bastiat== mocks protectionism in ==1845== with a famous text, the ==“Candlemakers' Petition”==: he has candle makers demand a law forcing everyone to close their windows and shutters, to protect them from the “unfair competition” of the sun, which provides light for free. The satire shows how absurd it is to want protection from something cheap.

Yet France returns to protectionism at the end of the century, with the ==Méline tariff== of 1892, which protects agriculture. The debate has never really stopped: every era replays the battle between those who want cheap goods and those who want to protect jobs and industries.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.7.tit: 1930: Smoot-Hawley, the law that made the crisis worse
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.7.par: After the 1929 crash, the US Congress wants to protect farmers and manufacturers. On ==June 17, 1930==, President Herbert Hoover signs the ==Smoot-Hawley Act==, which raises tariffs on ==more than 20,000 imported products==, to some of the highest levels in American history [15]. More than a thousand economists had signed a letter asking him not to.

The United States' partners protest, then retaliate with their own tariffs: Canada, European countries and many others. A recent study shows that US exports fall by 15 to 22% to the countries that protested, and by 28 to 33% to those that retaliated [15].

World trade collapses: according to an often-cited estimate, it falls by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934, although other calculations give a drop closer to one third in volume [15]. Historians agree on one point: ==Smoot-Hawley did not cause the Great Depression, but it made it worse and closed off markets that could have helped end it== [15].
This experience left its mark for decades: it explains why, after 1945, the major countries wanted to tie their own hands with common rules.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.8.tit: 1947-1995: from GATT to the WTO, the great decline
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.8.par: On ==October 30, 1947==, in Geneva, 23 countries sign the ==General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)== [16]. The principle is simple: negotiate tariff cuts together, and give all members the same advantages (the “most-favored-nation clause”).

Round after round of negotiations, the average tariffs of the major industrialized countries fall sharply, from about 22% in 1947 to about 5% after the Uruguay Round, concluded in 1994 [16]. This is one of the drivers of strong postwar growth.

On ==January 1, 1995==, the ==World Trade Organization (WTO)== replaces GATT [16]. It adds a real court to settle disputes between countries. On ==December 11, 2001==, China joins [16]: its integration into world trade transforms the global economy, with factories moving to Asia and prices falling everywhere.
Today, the WTO has more than 160 members. Its rules limit the tariffs each country can impose, with some exceptions (national security, dumping, unfair subsidies, safeguard measures).
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.9.tit: A tax that never dies: the “chicken tax”
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.9.par: In the early 1960s, France and West Germany tax American chicken, which is flooding their markets at low prices. Washington retaliates: through a proclamation in December 1963, which takes effect in ==January 1964==, President Lyndon Johnson imposes tariffs on four European products, including ==a 25% tax on imported light trucks== [17]. This is the “chicken war”.

More than sixty years later, the chicken dispute is forgotten and Germany no longer sells light trucks to the United States… but ==the 25% tax on imported pickup trucks still exists== [17]. It has shaped the American market: foreign manufacturers have built their pickups in the United States or Mexico, and some came up with clever tricks, like importing vans with rear seats that were removed on arrival to pay less [17].
The lesson: ==a tariff created for a temporary reason can last for decades==, because it creates interests (here, American pickup manufacturers, protected from competition) that fight to keep it.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.10.pa: The heart of the WTO is its dispute settlement system: a country that feels wronged files a complaint, a panel of experts rules, and the ruling can be appealed before an ==Appellate Body== of seven judges. For twenty years, this system made it possible to settle hundreds of trade conflicts without escalation.

But since 2017, the United States has been blocking the appointment of new judges, accusing the Appellate Body of overstepping its role [18]. On ==December 11, 2019==, only one judge is left: without a quorum, ==the Appellate Body can no longer function== [18]. A country that loses at first instance can now appeal “into the void” and block any decision.

To work around the deadlock, the European Union and other members created an interim arbitration mechanism in 2020. But the United States and China do not take part. As a result, trade conflicts are increasingly settled ==by force, with tariffs and retaliation, rather than by law==, as seen in the US-China trade war since 2018 and the 2025 “Liberation Day”.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.11.ti: The arguments for, the arguments against
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.11.pa: ==For tariffs==: protecting an ==infant industry== until it becomes competitive (this is how South Korea and the 19th-century United States industrialized), protecting ==strategic== sectors (steel, chips, medicines, defense), responding to competition seen as ==unfair== (subsidies, dumping), and preserving ==jobs== and regions.

==Against==: tariffs make ==consumers pay== (see above), raise the cost of ==imported parts== for domestic companies, invite ==retaliation==, and can protect ==inefficient== companies that no longer innovate. They often hit low-income households harder, since these spend a bigger share of their budget on imported goods.

Most economists conclude that ==tariffs are a costly tool for protecting jobs==, and that it is often better to help affected workers directly (training, retraining support). But rising geopolitical tensions have brought back the ==security== argument: depending on a rival for vital products can cost more than a tariff.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.11.ex: When you see an announcement, ask five questions: 1) Which product, and which country? 2) What rate, and starting when? 3) Who imports this product, and can they find it elsewhere? 4) Will the targeted country retaliate, and on what? 5) What is the legal basis (national security, dumping, emergency measure)? A weak basis can be struck down in court, as the US “IEEPA” tariffs were in February 2026.

dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.3.q: What does Ricardo's wine and cloth example (1817) show?
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.3.options: That you should produce everything yourself
That two countries gain from specializing and trading, even if one is better at everything
That wine is more profitable than cloth
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.3.explain: This is the theory of comparative advantage: you specialize where your disadvantage is smallest.

dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.4.options: It raised tariffs on more than 20,000 products and triggered retaliation
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.4.explain: It did not cause the crisis, but it made it worse by closing off markets.

dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.5.options: The United States is blocking the appointment of new judges
It was dissolved by a vote
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.5.explain: Without a quorum, a country that loses can appeal “into the void” and block the decision.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.6.q: What happened to the 25% US tax on light trucks created in 1964?
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.6.options: It was replaced by a tax on chicken
dossiers.droits-de-douane.quiz.6.explain: Born from a dispute with Europe over chicken, it still protects pickups built in the United States.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.hook: A metal box invented in 1956, a canal closed for eight years with fifteen ships trapped inside, a container ship stuck sideways for six days, a drought that holds up ships in Panama: a few dozen kilometers of sea are enough to send prices soaring around the world. Here's why.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.tldr.0: About 80% of goods traded worldwide travel by ship [1], thanks to a simple invention: the container, whose first voyage took place on April 26, 1956 [7].
dossiers.routes-maritimes.tldr.1: Many ships have to pass through a few very narrow straits and canals: Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez, Malacca, Panama. About one fifth of the world's oil passed through Hormuz before the 2026 crisis [2].
dossiers.routes-maritimes.tldr.2: Suez was closed from 1967 to 1975, trapping a “Yellow Fleet” of ships for eight years [5]; in March 2021, the Ever Given blocked it for six days, holding up about $9.6 billion of trade per day [4].
dossiers.routes-maritimes.tldr.3: After the Houthi attacks, Suez Canal revenue fell from $10.25 billion in 2023 to about $4 billion in 2024 [6]. In Panama, the 2023 drought brought the number of transits down to 22 ships per day [8].
dossiers.routes-maritimes.tldr.4: For China, about 80% of imported oil passes through the Strait of Malacca: this is the “Malacca dilemma”, formulated by President Hu Jintao in 2003 [9].
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.0.par: Before the 1950s, loading a ship was a huge job: dockworkers carried sacks, crates and barrels one by one. A ship could stay in port for a week. Transport was so expensive that it was rarely worth producing far from your customers.

An American trucker, ==Malcom McLean==, has a simple idea: put goods in large standard boxes that can be placed as they are on a truck, a train or a ship. On ==April 26, 1956==, his ship Ideal-X leaves Newark, near New York, for Houston with ==58 containers== on board [7]. On arrival, 58 trucks carry them away directly [7].

The cost of loading collapses: McLean calculates that it took about $5.8 per ton to load a ship by hand in 1956, and a fraction of that price with containers [7]. Ports are transformed, dockworkers disappear by the thousands, and it becomes profitable to make a phone in Asia to sell it in Europe.

That's why people often say that ==globalization fits in a box==. Today, about 80% of goods traded worldwide, by volume, travel by sea [1], and a large share of them in containers. But this efficiency has a weakness: everything goes through the same routes, and these routes have bottlenecks.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.1.par: Experts talk about ==“chokepoints”==: narrow passages that ships must use, or else make a huge detour. They can be natural straits (Hormuz, Malacca, Bab el-Mandeb, Gibraltar, the Bosphorus) or man-made canals (Suez, Panama).

They are dangerous for three reasons. ==An accident== can block them (a grounded ship). ==A conflict== can close them or make them too risky (mines, missiles, piracy). ==The climate== can make them impassable (drought, ice). In each case, ships wait or go around, and that is expensive.

The cost isn't limited to fuel. ==Crews== must be paid for longer, ==insurance== goes up in war zones, ==empty containers== end up stuck in the wrong place, and factories waiting for parts have to slow down. At the end of the chain, store prices go up.
Markets often react ==even before the blockage==. The mere threat of closing Hormuz is enough to push up the price of a barrel, because buyers hedge against the risk.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.2.tit: The Strait of Hormuz, the oil tap
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.2.par: Between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, the Strait of Hormuz carries about one fifth of the oil consumed worldwide [2], coming from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the Emirates, Kuwait or Qatar (for gas).
The slightest tension in the region moves markets: even without an actual blockade, the mere threat is enough to push up the price of a barrel.
In 2026, the feared scenario became reality: after US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran blocked the strait for months. A barrel went above $100 and diesel hit record prices in Europe [3].

There are a few bypasses: Saudi Arabia has a pipeline to the Red Sea, and the Emirates another to the port of Fujairah, which lies beyond the strait. But their capacity is not enough to replace all of Hormuz's traffic [2]. That's why most rich countries keep ==strategic oil reserves== (see our article on strategic reserves).
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.3.par: The Suez Canal, in Egypt, has linked the Mediterranean to the Red Sea since 1869: it is the shortcut between Europe and Asia that avoids going around Africa. To reach it from the south, ships must pass through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, off Yemen.

==July 1956==: Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalizes the canal, until then run by a French-British company. France, the United Kingdom and Israel attack Egypt, but have to withdraw under pressure from the United States and the USSR [10]. It marks the end of the era when London and Paris could act alone in the Middle East.

==June 1967==: during the Six-Day War, Egypt closes the canal. It stays closed for ==eight years, until June 1975== [5]. About fifteen merchant ships are trapped in the Great Bitter Lake, in the middle of the canal. Covered in sand, they are nicknamed the ==“Yellow Fleet”==. Their crews get organized, set up an association, a sailing club and even “Olympic Games” in 1968 [5]. Only two ships leave under their own power in 1975 [5].
During those eight years, the world adapts: oil companies build ==supertankers==, too big for Suez, which go around Africa profitably. A crisis can thus change the shape of trade for good.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.4.tit: March 2021: six days with the Ever Given stuck sideways
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.4.par: On ==March 23, 2021==, in strong winds, the 400-meter-long container ship Ever Given runs aground sideways across the Suez Canal. Nothing can get through. It takes six days of dredging and towing to free it, on ==March 29== [4].
Meanwhile, more than 300 ships line up on either side of the canal [4]. According to estimates, about ==$9.6 billion of goods per day== are held up [4]. Some shipowners decide to go around Africa.

The effects last much longer than six days: the ships all arrive at the same time in European ports, which become congested, and containers run short in Asia. In a world of ==“just-in-time”== supply, where companies keep very little stock, a single ship is enough to disrupt factories on several continents.
The image of the giant stuck on a sandbank became the symbol of the ==fragility of global supply chains==, just when Covid had already weakened them.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.4.pla: how a grounded ship pushes up a price
The Ever Given blocks Suez for six days; hundreds of ships wait [4].
Containers arrive late in Europe, then all at once: ports become congested.
Empty containers stay stuck in Europe while Asia runs short of them: the price of shipping a container climbs.
Companies pay more for transport and pass part of it on to their selling prices.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.5.tit: The Red Sea since 2023: the big detour
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.5.par: In late 2023, in connection with the war in Gaza, Yemen's Houthi rebels start attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea with missiles and drones. Between November 2023 and January 2024, more than 100 ships are targeted, two are sunk and four sailors are killed [6].
Many shipowners prefer to go around Africa via the Cape of Good Hope, adding about 10 to 14 days to the journey. In 2024, only about 13,200 ships use the Suez Canal, ==half as many as in 2023== [6].

For Egypt, it's a shock: the canal is one of its main sources of foreign currency. Its revenue falls ==from a record $10.25 billion in 2023 to about $4 billion in 2024== [6]. A country that is not at war thus loses more than half of a vital resource because of a neighboring conflict.
This crisis shows that control over a chokepoint doesn't belong only to states: ==a non-state armed group, with limited means, can disrupt world trade==.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.6.par: The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is the great highway between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. A large share of the trade and oil bound for China, Japan and Korea passes through it.

On ==November 29, 2003==, Chinese President Hu Jintao voices his concern to Party leaders: about ==four fifths of the oil imported by China passes through this strait== [9]. If a hostile power, in practice the US Navy, closed it during a crisis (around Taiwan, for example), China could run short of energy. The press calls this problem the ==“Malacca dilemma”== [9].

Since then, China has been looking for workarounds: oil and gas pipelines from Russia, Central Asia and Myanmar, deep-water ports in Pakistan (Gwadar) and elsewhere as part of the “New Silk Roads”, strategic oil reserves, and a fast-growing navy.
Malacca shows that a strait is not just an economic issue: it is ==a lever of power==. Whoever can close it, or protect it, influences the strategy of others.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.7.tit: Panama: when the climate closes a canal
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.7.par: The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, links the Atlantic to the Pacific. Unlike Suez, it is not at sea level: ships go up and down through locks, which run on ==fresh water from Gatún Lake==. Each transit drains a large amount of water from the lake into the sea.

In 2023, a drought made worse by the El Niño climate phenomenon lowers the lake's level. The canal authority has to limit the number of ships and their loads: in November 2023, only ==22 ships per day== get through, whereas a normal day can see around forty [8].

Ships wait for weeks, some pay very high prices at auction to pass earlier, others take the detour via Suez or Cape Horn. ==Proof that the climate too can disrupt world trade==. In 2026, with a new El Niño episode, the authority again reduced transits, to 32 per day in September [8].
Panama is studying the creation of a new reservoir to secure the canal's water. But residents need water too: ==world trade and drinking water are competing==.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.8.par: Since 1945, it is mainly ==the US Navy== that has guaranteed freedom of navigation on the major sea routes, with fleets deployed in the Mediterranean, the Gulf and the Pacific. Trading countries benefit from this security, often without paying for it.

This situation is changing. ==China== has greatly expanded its navy and is developing ports along its trade routes. ==India== keeps watch over the Indian Ocean. Countries such as ==France== or the United Kingdom maintain bases and protection missions, like the European operation Aspides in the Red Sea from 2024.

Law matters too. The ==United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea== (1982) guarantees ships “transit passage” through international straits, even when they cross a state's waters. But some countries, like Iran for Hormuz, have not ratified this text and dispute this interpretation.
Remember that ==the sea is free as long as someone protects it==. When powers clash, chokepoints become the first places where pressure is applied.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.sections.9.par: With global warming, Arctic ice melts in summer, and a ==Northern Sea Route== along the Russian coast becomes passable for part of the year. It greatly shortens the journey between Asia and Europe, but it is controlled by Russia, expensive (icebreakers, insurance) and risky for the environment.

Countries and companies are also trying to ==reduce their dependence on bottlenecks==: bringing part of production closer to home (“nearshoring”), using more suppliers, keeping more stock, developing rail links between China and Europe. These solutions cost more than the “all just-in-time” approach of before 2020.

Finally, ==the undersea cables== that carry the internet often follow the same routes and pass through the same straits (see our article on undersea cables). So a chokepoint is not just a route for goods: it is also a route for data.
dossiers.routes-maritimes.forMe: When you see the price of gas or of an imported product jump, look at the map: a crisis in a faraway strait may be the cause. And when a company announces delivery delays, ask yourself which passage its goods were supposed to go through.

dossiers.semi-conducteurs.hook: Your phone, your car and artificial intelligence depend on tiny chips made largely on a single island. How did an object invented in 1947 become the focus of a rivalry between the United States and China, why did Japan lose its place, and why do people talk about a “silicon shield”?
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.tldr.0: Semiconductors (or chips) are the “brain” of almost every electronic device. The first microprocessor, the 1971 Intel 4004, had about 2,300 transistors; a 2024 Nvidia AI chip has 208 billion [5].
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.tldr.1: In 2021, 92% of the production capacity for the most advanced chips (below 10 nanometers) was in Taiwan, the rest in South Korea [3]. TSMC, founded in 1987, is the giant of the sector.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.tldr.2: The 2021 shortage cost the auto industry about $210 billion in sales and meant 7.7 million cars were not built [6].
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.tldr.3: Since October 7, 2022, the United States has sharply restricted China's access to advanced chips and machines [7]; in August 2023, Huawei surprises everyone with a phone using a Chinese chip made at 7 nanometers [8].
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.tldr.4: The United States (CHIPS Act, $52.7 billion, August 2022) and Europe (European Chips Act, more than 43 billion euros, target of 20% of the world market by 2030) subsidize their factories [2][9].
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.0.par: Making a chip involves several countries: design is often American (Nvidia, Apple, Qualcomm), the most cutting-edge machines are Dutch (ASML is the world's only maker of EUV lithography machines), and the finest chips are manufactured in Taiwan.
This specialization is very efficient, but it creates weak points: if one link breaks, the whole chain stops. The 2021 chip shortage, for example, halted car factories around the world.

A chip goes through hundreds of steps: it starts with an ==ultra-pure silicon disk== (the “wafer”), on which circuits are etched layer by layer using light, chemicals and gases. The factories, called ==“fabs”==, cost more than $20 billion for the most modern ones and must be cleaner than an operating room.

No country masters the whole chain. The United States dominates design and design software, Japan and Europe the machines and chemicals, Taiwan and South Korea advanced manufacturing, and China assembly and simpler chips [3]. ==Each country holds part of the hostage.==
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.1.tit: 1947-1971: from the transistor to the microprocessor
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.1.par: It all starts in ==December 1947== at Bell Labs, near New York: three researchers, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley, develop the ==transistor==, a tiny electrical switch with no moving parts. It replaces vacuum tubes, which were big, fragile and power-hungry. They will receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956.

In the late 1950s, Jack Kilby (Texas Instruments) and Robert Noyce (Fairchild) come up with the idea of etching several transistors onto the same plate: this is the ==integrated circuit==, the first “chip”. Shockley moves to California; his former employees found Fairchild, then Intel: ==Silicon Valley== is born.

In 1965, Gordon Moore, future co-founder of Intel, notices that the number of transistors on a chip doubles at regular intervals. This ==“Moore's law”==, which is an observation and not a law of physics, guides the industry for fifty years: roughly every two years, chips become twice as dense.

On November 15, 1971, Intel launches the ==4004==, the first microprocessor sold to the public: about ==2,300 transistors== [5]. In 2024, Nvidia's Blackwell chip, designed for artificial intelligence, has ==208 billion== [5], about 90 million times more.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.1.pla: A transistor is a tiny switch: it lets current through (1) or blocks it (0).
By combining thousands of switches, you can add, compare and store information: this is the binary language of computers.
The smaller the transistors, the more you can fit on a chip, and the faster it computes while using little power.
From about 2,300 transistors in 1971 to 208 billion in 2024 [5]: this is what made smartphones and AI possible.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.2.par: It has been forgotten, but in the 1980s the world leader in chips is not Taiwan: it is ==Japan==. Its giants (NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, Fujitsu) produce high-quality memory chips at low prices. Between 1980 and 1989, Japan's share of the world market rises from about 27% to 52%, while the United States' share falls from 57% to 35% [10].

Washington sees this as a threat to its security: the US military depends on Japanese chips. On ==September 2, 1986==, under US pressure, Japan signs a semiconductor agreement: it commits to stop selling below cost abroad and to open its market to foreign chips [10]. In 1987, the United States even imposes 100% tariffs on certain Japanese electronic products.

In the following years, Japan's industry declines, squeezed between the agreements, the bursting of its financial bubble and the rise of Korean (Samsung) and Taiwanese competitors. ==This is an important precedent==: the United States had already used trade to slow down a technological rival, long before China.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.3.tit: 1987: TSMC and the invention of the “foundry”
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.3.par: In 1987, in Taiwan, engineer ==Morris Chang==, a Texas Instruments veteran, founds TSMC with the support of the Taiwanese state. His idea is new: design ==no chips under its own name== and manufacture other companies' chips. This is the ==“pure-play foundry”== model: TSMC never competes with its customers [4].

This model frees inventors: a company can design chips without spending tens of billions on a factory. Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm become “fabless” companies, which hand manufacturing over to TSMC.

By devoting itself entirely to manufacturing, TSMC builds up experience that no one can match. In 2021, according to the US industry association and the consulting firm BCG, ==92% of the world's production capacity for the most advanced chips== (below 10 nanometers) is in Taiwan, and the remaining 8% in South Korea [3]. Intel, the former king, has fallen behind.
Hence the often-heard phrase: ==the world's most advanced chips are made on an island of 36,000 km², about 130 km from mainland China.==
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.4.par: China considers Taiwan part of its territory and does not rule out taking control of it. The United States, for its part, supports the island militarily.

A crisis around Taiwan would therefore not just be a regional conflict: it could deprive the world of most of its advanced chips. Some talk about a ==“silicon shield”==: TSMC's importance would protect the island, because no one has an interest in its production stopping.

This shield has its limits. A chip factory can't be captured like an oil well: it depends on foreign machines, spare parts, software and engineers. In the event of an invasion, it would probably stop on its own. Some US officials have even raised the idea of making the factories unusable rather than letting them fall into Beijing's hands.
To reduce the risk, TSMC is also building factories abroad: in Arizona in the United States, in Japan, and in Dresden in Germany. But the most advanced chips are still produced mainly in Taiwan.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.5.par: At the start of the pandemic, in 2020, carmakers cancel their chip orders, expecting to sell fewer cars. At the same time, everyone is buying computers, consoles and phones for remote work. Chipmakers reallocate their production.

When demand for cars picks up again, there are no chips left. A modern car contains hundreds of them, for the brakes, windows, screen or engine. Factories stop, and nearly finished cars wait in parking lots. According to the consulting firm AlixPartners, the shortage costs carmakers about ==$210 billion in sales== in 2021 and prevents ==7.7 million vehicles== from being built [6].

The crisis has several combined causes: demand linked to remote work and 5G, factories hit by fires or droughts, and US sanctions against Huawei, which pushed companies to stockpile chips massively [6]. It shows governments that ==chips worth a few dollars can block entire industries==.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.6.tit: The chip war between Washington and Beijing
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.6.par: On ==October 7, 2022==, the US Department of Commerce publishes unprecedented export rules: it bans selling China the most powerful AI chips, the machines for making advanced chips, and even help from American engineers to cutting-edge Chinese factories [7]. The Netherlands and Japan, which make the essential machines, follow with their own restrictions.

The goal is clear: ==prevent China from catching up== in the finest chips, which are essential for AI and weapons. China retaliates by restricting, from summer 2023, its exports of gallium and germanium, two metals used in electronics of which it is the leading producer.

On ==August 29, 2023==, a bombshell: Huawei launches the Mate 60 Pro, a phone with a chip designed by its subsidiary HiSilicon and ==made in China by SMIC, at 7 nanometers== [8]. The controls were meant precisely to keep China from going below 10 nanometers [8]. SMIC managed it with older machines, at the cost of a lower yield.

The debate remains open: do the restrictions really slow China down, or do they push it to develop its own industry faster? Probably both: China is still behind on the most advanced chips, but is investing huge sums so it no longer depends on other countries.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.6.pla: why a Dutch machine matters so much
To etch the finest chips, you need extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light, produced by machines from ASML, the world's only maker.
The Netherlands, an ally of the United States, bans selling these machines to China.
Without them, Chinese factories have to use older machines several times in a row to etch finer: it's possible, but slower and more expensive.
China reaches 7 nanometers in 2023 [8], but remains behind TSMC, which is already producing finer chips at scale.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.7.par: The United States passes the ==CHIPS and Science Act in August 2022==: $52.7 billion for manufacturing, research and training, including $39 billion in aid for factories [9]. Intel, TSMC, Samsung and Micron announce factories on American soil.

The European Union responds with the ==European Chips Act==, approved in 2023: it aims to mobilize more than ==43 billion euros== in public and private investment, with the goal of doubling Europe's share of the world market to reach ==20% by 2030== [2][9]. Europe today accounts for only about 10% of the market or less, depending on estimates [9].

These plans raise doubts: much of the European money is not new but redeployed from other budgets [9], factories lack engineers, and some projects have been postponed. Building a factory takes years, and catching up with TSMC would take even longer.

Japan, South Korea, India and China have also launched their own plans. This is a turning point: after thirty years of globalization in which everyone specialized, ==states want to produce at home what they consider vital==, even if it costs more.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.sections.8.par: Since the arrival of large artificial intelligence models, demand for specialized chips has exploded. Nvidia's ==graphics processors==, originally designed for video games, turn out to be perfect for training these models, because they perform thousands of calculations in parallel.

Nvidia, which does not make its own chips (TSMC does that [5]), becomes one of the most valuable companies in the world. Big tech companies spend tens of billions of dollars a year on data centers filled with these chips.

This rush further strengthens Taiwan's role and the geopolitical tension: the most powerful AI chips are precisely the ones the United States bans from export to China [7]. ==Chips have become to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th==: a resource on which power depends, and which states want to control.
dossiers.semi-conducteurs.forMe: Every time you buy a phone, a console or a car, part of its price and availability depends on a few factories in Taiwan and on machines made in the Netherlands. When you hear about tensions in the Taiwan Strait or new chip restrictions, your future purchases are at stake too.

dossiers.sanctions.hook: An oil embargo that pushes Japan toward Pearl Harbor, sanctions against Mussolini's Italy that forget… oil, Iranian banks cut off from SWIFT, a French bank fined $8.9 billion, and 300 billion in frozen Russian reserves. How do sanctions work, since when, and do they really work?
dossiers.sanctions.tldr.0: An economic sanction is a measure that cuts off or limits trade with a country, a company or a person in order to apply pressure.
dossiers.sanctions.tldr.1: After the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the West froze about $300 billion of the Russian central bank's reserves and cut several Russian banks off from the SWIFT system [1]; on December 5, 2022, the G7 and the EU capped the price of Russian oil at $60 per barrel [8].
dossiers.sanctions.tldr.2: History is full of failed sanctions: in 1935, the League of Nations sanctions Italy but forgets oil [4]; in 1941, the US oil embargo against Japan comes before Pearl Harbor [5].
